lessons.title: Letters of application
lessons.programRef: Form 3 English Language (to be checked against the official programme)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Set out a letter of application.
Present qualities, skills and experience persuasively.
Use a polite closing and mention your availability.
reviewNotes: Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.md: A **letter of application** is a formal letter in which you ask for a job, a place or an opportunity: a holiday job, a scholarship, a place in a club. It must convince the reader that you are suitable. A typical task: *Apply for the post of library assistant advertised on the school notice board.*

blocks.title: Layout and structure
blocks.md:
Use the formal layout (your address, date, receiver's address, *Dear Sir/Madam*, subject line, *Yours faithfully*). Structure:
1. **Paragraph 1:** the post you apply for and where you saw it.
2. **Paragraph 2:** your **qualifications and qualities** (age, class, results, skills).
3. **Paragraph 3:** your **experience or interests**, and why you are suitable.
4. **Paragraph 4:** availability, readiness for an interview, polite thanks.

blocks.caption: Each paragraph has a job to do.
blocks.alt: A diagram with Application at the top and three arrows to Post (where seen), About me (skills, class) and Close (available, thanks).

blocks.title: Style
blocks.md:
- Be **truthful**, specific and positive: *I have served as library prefect for a year* is better than *I am very good*.
- Avoid begging (*please, I am very poor*) and boasting.
- Use formal language and correct spelling.
- Write **only relevant** information: no family history.
- Never invent qualifications.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Forgetting to say **which post** you apply for and **where** you saw the advertisement.
- Writing the whole life story.
- Using *Yours sincerely* with *Dear Sir/Madam*.
- Telling the reader what he must do instead of showing politeness.
- Leaving out availability or contact information.

blocks.title: Example 1: the opening
blocks.statement: Write the opening paragraph of an application for the post of library assistant advertised on the school notice board of GHS Limbe.
steps: State the post, the source and the purpose.
*I am writing to apply for the post of library assistant, as advertised on the notice board of Government High School, Limbe, on 3 June.*
blocks.answer: I am writing to apply for the post of library assistant, as advertised on the notice board of Government High School, Limbe, on 3 June.

blocks.title: Example 2: a convincing paragraph
blocks.statement: Write a short paragraph showing that you are suitable.
steps: Give a quality + proof: responsible (library prefect), organised, reads a lot.
*I am a Form 3 pupil and have served as library prefect for one year. I am responsible, well organised and I enjoy reading.*
blocks.answer: I am a Form 3 pupil and have served as library prefect for one year. I am responsible, well organised and I enjoy reading.

lessons.title: Writing a report
lessons.programRef: Form 3 English Language (to be checked against the official programme)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Set out a report with a title, headings and recommendations.
Write in the past tense for events and present for findings, in a formal style.
reviewNotes: Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.md: A **report** gives an organised account of an event, a visit or a problem for a specific reader (the principal, the class, a club). It is **factual, clear and formal**. Typical tasks: *a report on the school sports day*, *a report on the state of the school library*.

blocks.title: Layout and sections
blocks.md:
**Heading:** *REPORT ON THE STATE OF THE SCHOOL LIBRARY*; below it: **To / From / Date** (or *Prepared by*).
1. **Introduction (terms of reference):** purpose and how the information was collected.
2. **Findings** (body): short paragraphs or numbered points, under headings.
3. **Conclusion:** a short summary of what the findings show.
4. **Recommendations:** what should be done, in order of importance.
Sign off with your name and position.

blocks.caption: Use clear headings so the reader finds each part quickly.
blocks.alt: A flowchart of the parts of a report: heading, introduction, findings, conclusion and recommendations.

blocks.title: Style
blocks.md:
- **Facts, not feelings**: *Only 40 books were found for 300 pupils* (not *The library is terrible*).
- Use the **past tense** for what you did or saw and the **present** for conclusions.
- Use **impersonal, formal** language; short, clear sentences.
- **Number or bullet** the findings and recommendations.
- Do not invent details beyond those in the task; keep numbers realistic.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Writing a **story** or letter instead of a report.
- No title or headings.
- Opinions instead of facts, or insulting language.
- Recommendations that do not follow from the findings.
- Forgetting the date, the writer or the reader.

blocks.title: Example 1: the heading
blocks.statement: Write the heading of a report by a prefect to the principal on the Form 3 clean-up campaign held on 12 May.
steps: Give a title in capitals, then **To / From / Date**.
blocks.answer:
REPORT ON THE FORM 3 CLEAN-UP CAMPAIGN HELD ON 12 MAY
To: The Principal
From: The Senior Prefect
Date: 14 May 2026

blocks.title: Example 2: fact or opinion
blocks.statement: Which is suitable for a report: (a) The library is a disgrace. (b) The library has only 40 books for 300 pupils.

lessons.title: Writing and giving a speech
lessons.programRef: Form 3 English Language (to be checked against the official programme)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Open and close a speech with the correct forms of address.
Use persuasive devices: rhetorical questions, repetition and the rule of three.
Plan a speech for a particular audience.
reviewNotes: Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.md: A **speech** is written to be **heard**. It addresses an audience directly, so it uses a personal, lively style. Typical tasks: *a speech to welcome a guest*, *a speech on the importance of reading*, *a speech for a debate*.

blocks.title: Structure and form of address
blocks.md:
1. **Salutation:** *Madam Principal, teachers, ladies and gentlemen, fellow pupils,* (the most important person first).
2. **Introduction:** greet, say who you are, state the topic.
3. **Body:** two or three main points, each with a reason or example.
4. **Conclusion:** summarise, appeal to action, thank the audience: *Thank you for listening.*
Write the **title** above: *SPEECH ON THE IMPORTANCE OF READING*.

blocks.title: Persuasive devices
blocks.md:
- **Rhetorical question:** *How can we build our country if we do not read?*
- **Repetition:** *We must read; we must learn; we must lead.*
- **Rule of three:** *honest, hardworking and brave.*
- **Direct address:** *you, we, let us...*
- **Facts and examples** that the audience can check.
Keep sentences **short and clear** so that listeners can follow.

blocks.caption: The body is where you persuade; the closing is what people remember.
blocks.alt: A diagram with Speech at the top and three arrows to Opening (greet, topic), Body (points, proof) and Closing (appeal, thanks).

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Forgetting the salutation or the title.
- Writing it like an essay, with long, complex sentences.
- Facts that are exaggerated or invented.
- Only opinions without reasons.
- Ending abruptly without thanking the audience.

blocks.title: Example 1: salutation
blocks.statement: Write a suitable salutation for a speech given to the principal, teachers and pupils at the school assembly.
steps: The most senior person first, then the others.

blocks.title: Example 2: a rhetorical question
blocks.statement: Write a rhetorical question for a speech against littering.
steps: Ask a question whose answer is obvious.
blocks.answer: How can we be proud of our school when our compound is covered in rubbish?

lessons.title: The argumentative essay
lessons.programRef: Form 3 English Language (to be checked against the official programme)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Plan an essay for or against a motion.
Develop paragraphs with a point, a reason and an example.
Write a balanced introduction and conclusion.
reviewNotes: Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.md: An **argumentative essay** presents your opinion on a topic and persuades the reader with reasons and examples. A typical title: *Pupils should not be allowed to use mobile phones at school. Discuss.* A good essay is **organised** and **fair**: it considers the other side before explaining why your view is stronger.

blocks.title: Plan in four steps
blocks.md:
1. **Introduction:** explain the topic and state your position (thesis) clearly.
2. **Body:** 2 or 3 paragraphs, each with a **point** (topic sentence), a **reason** and an **example**.
3. **Counter-argument:** one paragraph on the opposite view and why it is weaker.
4. **Conclusion:** restate your position in new words and give a final thought.

blocks.caption: Each body paragraph proves one point.
blocks.alt: A flowchart: introduction with topic and position, argument one with point reason and example, argument two with the other side, then a conclusion that restates and closes.

blocks.title: Persuasive language
blocks.md: Useful phrases: *In my opinion..., Firstly, ... Moreover, ... In addition, ... However, some people argue that ... but ..., Therefore, ... In conclusion...* Use **facts and examples** drawn from Cameroonian life. Avoid insulting people and extreme words (*always, never, everyone*).

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Taking no clear side or changing sides.
- Reasons with no examples.
- One long paragraph.
- Repeating the same point in different words.
- Emotional, rude or exaggerated language.
- Introducing new arguments in the conclusion.

blocks.title: Example 1: a thesis
blocks.statement: Write a thesis sentence for an essay *Pupils should wear school uniform.*
steps: Take a clear position and hint at the reasons.
*I strongly believe that pupils should wear school uniform because it promotes equality, discipline and school pride.*
blocks.answer: I strongly believe that pupils should wear school uniform because it promotes equality, discipline and school pride.

blocks.title: Example 2: point, reason, example
blocks.statement: Develop the point *School uniform promotes equality.*
steps: Reason: it hides differences in family wealth.
Example: in one classroom pupils from rich and poor homes look alike.
blocks.answer: School uniform promotes equality. It hides differences in family wealth, so that pupils from richer and poorer homes look alike and no one is laughed at because of his or her clothes.

Ngu Tabi, P.O. Box 55, Buea, 10 July 2026
The Manager, Mama Ada's Shop, Buea Town
Dear Madam,
APPLICATION FOR THE POST OF SHOP ASSISTANT
I am writing to apply for the holiday post of shop assistant advertised on your shop door on 8 July.
I am a Form 3 pupil of Government Bilingual High School, Buea. I am honest, hard-working and good at mathematics, and I have helped in my aunt's shop for two holidays, where I served customers and kept the accounts.
I am available from 20 July to 31 August and can attend an interview at any time. Thank you for considering my application.
Yours faithfully,
Ngu Tabi

exercises.source: Original exercise written for CastBridge, in the style of the curriculum
exercises.prompt: You are the secretary of the school Environment Club. Write a short report (about 150 words) to the principal on a tree-planting activity held on Saturday 10 May in which 40 pupils planted 60 seedlings near the football field. Include findings and two recommendations.
exercises.model:
REPORT ON THE TREE-PLANTING ACTIVITY OF 10 MAY
To: The Principal
From: The Secretary, Environment Club
Date: 12 May 2026
Introduction: This report describes the tree-planting activity held on Saturday 10 May near the football field.
Findings: 1. Forty pupils took part. 2. Sixty seedlings were planted. 3. The soil was dry, so each seedling was watered.
Conclusion: The activity was successful and the pupils worked with enthusiasm.
Recommendations: 1. The seedlings should be watered twice a week. 2. A fence should be built to protect them.
Secretary, Environment Club

exercises.source: Original exercise written for CastBridge, in the style of the curriculum
exercises.prompt: Write a speech of about 200 words to be given at the school assembly on *Why every pupil should read for 30 minutes a day*. Include a salutation, a rhetorical question and a conclusion with thanks.
exercises.model:
SPEECH ON READING
Madam Principal, teachers, fellow pupils,
Good morning. Today I want to talk about reading. How can we expect to learn if we never open a book?
Reading builds our vocabulary, improves our spelling and opens our minds to the world. A pupil who reads for thirty minutes a day will write better, speak better and understand better. Moreover, a book is cheaper than a ticket to anywhere, yet it can take us everywhere.
Some will say, 'I have no time.' But we find time for football, for films and for our phones. We can find thirty minutes for a book.
Let us read: in the morning, in the evening, at home and at school. Thank you for listening.

exercises.prompt: Write a plan (not the full essay) for: *Farming should be taught in every secondary school. Discuss.* Give the thesis, two arguments with reasons and examples, one counter-argument and the conclusion.
exercises.model: Thesis: Farming should be taught in every secondary school. Argument 1: it teaches useful skills (growing maize, keeping hens; many pupils will farm). Argument 2: it reduces hunger and teaches discipline (school garden can feed the canteen). Counter-argument: some say it takes time from academic subjects, but it can be taught in a few hours a week. Conclusion: farming skills build a strong economy and should be taught.
rubric: 2 marks: two arguments with reasons and examples.
